newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish truckers open borders after four-day siege.
newsitem.headline: Danish truckers open borders after four-day siege.

text.p: Danish truckers ended a four-day blockade on Thursday of seaports and a land border with Germany, that has seriously disrupted domestic and export trade.

About 2,000 drivers voted overwhelmingly at their make-shift protest headquarters at the Padborg border crossing to end the protest over travel allowances, after leaders warned that adverse public opinion was growing, a participant told Reuters.
"I see this as a victory...we have focused attention on our case," drivers' spokesman Ole Prusse told Danish Radio.
The blockade, of goods traffic only, was not related to nationwide protests by French truckers.
Tax Minister Carsten Koch welcomed the truckers' decision while criticising their protest methods.
"It is a good and worthy decision," he said, adding that he understood that from the drivers' point of view officials had taken too long in drafting new allowance levels.
"But they were wrong from the start, disruption is not the right weapon with which to resolve such a conflict," he said.
Joergen Eliassen, deputy head of the Danish Road Haulage Association representing the drivers' employers, said that violence was not the way to go about tax reform.
"Others use parliamentary methods," he told the Danish news agency Ritzau.

Drivers started the blockade on Monday to back their demands for a daily 500 crown tax allowance for foreign trips. On Wednesday they rejected Koch's offer of 250 crowns and their position on Thursday night was still unclear.

Police at Padborg border crossing said drivers started returning to their vehicles just after 2000 GMT, but some had uncoupled their trailers and it would probably take several hours for the last of some 2,000 lorries to leave.

"We are regulating traffic to prevent chaos and it will, take time before conditions are normal again. Trucks should not count on getting in or out of the country before dawn," a duty officer at Padborg police told Ritzau news agency.
State-run radio said that drivers blocking seaports around the country also started to clear the quaysides as word of the Padborg vote spread.

The Danish protest halted most movement of goods between Denmark, Britain, Germany, Norway and Sweden and paralysed shipments from the Jutland peninsula, where most food is produced, to the capital, Copenhagen, on the island of Zealand.
Workers at fish and meat processing plants were sent home as the supply of raw materials was cut off along with access to markets for finished products.
Nearly a million Christmas trees tightly packed on 600 lorries were believed to have rotted stranded at Padborg along with shipments of milk, cheese and meat, producers' organisations said.
The siege also sent shockwaves abroad, combining with the French action to threaten production at Sweden's Volvo and Saab vehicle manufacturers.
